summary: Maine's Moose Peak Light on Mistake Island, lit 1826 or 1827, with the most fog of any station in 1928; privately owned since 2012.

lens.where: U.S. Coast Guard Exhibit Center, Forrestville, Maryland

structures.note: Shape conical; base masonry and stone (USLHS).
First tower, replaced by the brick tower of 1851 (LighthouseFriends).
Destroyed in a 1982 Coast Guard demolition exercise (LighthouseFriends).
LighthouseFriends gives 1913; USLHS gives 1912 for the building.

access.note: Privately owned; grounds open and tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Went into service 9 October 1826 (LighthouseFriends); the Society's record gives 1827.
Original tower refitted and a new brick tower built; focal plane raised to 65 ft.
Iron watchroom and second-order lantern room added; lens relit around 5 September 1888.
Brick cistern built in the cellar of the assistant keeper's house (Board report).
Keeper and son rescued the crew of the Nova Scotian schooner Ashton on 26 November 1896.
First-class reed horn in a brick fog-signal building (LighthouseFriends); USLHS gives 1912.
Keepers' double dwelling destroyed in a Coast Guard demolition training exercise.
Fresnel lens replaced by a modern optic; the lens is in storage.
Auction closed 1 November 2012 with a winning bid of $93,500.
Donated to a non-profit medical building society.
Bought by a private couple for $150,000.

wrecks.outcome: Wrecked on Man Island near Mistake Island; crew of four; captain taken to Jonesport; old vessel a total wreck, cargo saved.

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left open for a human: (1) first light 1826 (LighthouseFriends; Wikipedia lead) against 1827 (USLHS place record and the record's first_lit); (2) fog-signal building 1912 (USLHS) against 1913 (LighthouseFriends); (3) the 2012 auction (LighthouseFriends, closed 1 Nov 2012) against 'January 2013' in the Wikipedia lead, which is not cited. Fog years (fact-check 2026-10-28): the 1928 Bulletin table is for fiscal 1928 (the year to June 1928) and says the fog signal operated 1,934 hours, 22 per cent of the year. The 1930 Bulletin (PDF p. 5) tabulates fiscal 1929 and gives Moose Peak 1,562 hours; the 1931 Bulletin (PDF p. 7) gives 1,691 hours for the year ending 30 June 1930. LighthouseFriends dates the 1,562 figure to 1930; the story follows the Bulletin. The 1928 entry words its figure as hours the fog signal operated and the later ones as hours of fog, so the three figures are not averaged. The 1894 whistle passage (fiscal 1894, scan p. 721) is about the Libby Islands whistle; the keeper's sentence says 'the whistle' and the reading is taken from the paragraph. Check the page image before publishing. The 1885 Board report quotation is not in the corpus: the story attributes it to LighthouseFriends, which quotes the Board. The story no longer says Congress appropriated $10,000; the source says Congress appropriated 'the requested amount' and separately gives the Board's 1885 estimate of $10,000. The 1928 Bulletin OCR is damaged ('Dperated'); the figure 1,934 and the phrase 'the greatest amount of fog recorded' are read from the page at PDF p. 37. The 1883 life-saving entry gives day and month only; the year 1883 is inferred from the report's fiscal year (July 1883 to June 1884). Vessel name 'Ashton' comes from LighthouseFriends only: the Board's FY1900 text is OCR-damaged ('Ashioii, of Weymouth, Nova Scotia'). Keeper's name spelled Dobbin (USLHS roster) and Dobbins (Board reports, LighthouseFriends); the roster and the Board are not linked beyond the name. The keepers roster has 96 lines printed exactly by USLHS; several spans carry 'at least'. Keepers whose service ended after about 1960 appear only as the archive prints them. The 2019 buyers are private individuals and are not named. Wikipedia is used only as a lead and is not cited. No photos were added.
